item.title: European stocks close lower across the board as bond yields climb
item.description:
As London/European traders head home, the major European stock indices are closing lower across the board. Italy and Spain led the declines, but there was little separation, with all five major markets falling more than 1%. Not a good day. 

The closing snapshot showed:

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,319.78, down 302.84 points or 1.18%.

  • France’s CAC: 7,868.06, down 88.63 points or 1.11%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: 10,764.70, down 117.21 points or 1.08%.

  • Spain’s Ibex: 19,039.30, down 287.00 points or 1.49%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 49,086.28, down 770.89 points or 1.55%.

After last week’s gains, sellers had their say to start the new trading week.

European Bond yields move higher with France leading the way. 

European benchmark 10-year yields moved higher, with France leading the way:

  • Germany: 3.456%, up 3.6 basis points.

  • France: 4.940%, up 8.6 basis points.

  • UK: 5.443%, up 3.9 basis points.

  • Spain: 4.080%, up 3.0 basis points.

  • Italy: 4.582%, up 5.0 basis points.

The French move stands out. Its yield rose 5 basis points more than Germany’s, widening the spread between the two countries. France's 10 year yield is near the highest level going back to May 2002.

There is a key budget vote in France set for tomorrow. The National Assembly is scheduled to hold a formal vote on the first part of the budget bill, covering government revenues, after parliamentary questions. The full budget vote is scheduled for November 17.

Tomorrow's vote matters as a test of the government's ability to deliver fiscal consolidation. A smooth passage would offer some relief and give the euro a boost, while a rejection or major concessions that weaken the deficit-reduction plan could put further pressure on French bonds and the euro.

US stocks rebound, led by the Nasdaq

As European traders head home, US stocks are trading higher, with the Nasdaq indices leading the way. The Dow is near unchanged, highlighting the stronger buying in technology shares.

The latest snapshot shows:

  • Dow industrial average: 52,010.19, up 2.98 points or 0.01%.

  • S&P 500: 7,708.59, up 49.15 points or 0.64%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: 26,523.44, up 383.41 points or 1.47%.

  • Nasdaq 100: 29,671.88, up 484.34 points or 1.66%.

  • Russell 2000: 2,734.95, up 13.58 points or 0.50%.

After last week’s technology-led selling, buyers are taking a shot at a recovery. The Nasdaq 100 is leading the rebound, but one stronger session is only a start. Buyers now need follow-through to build confidence that the recovery has more room to run.

US Treasury yields were also higher at the snapshot:

  • 2-year: 4.776%, up 4.0 basis points.

  • 5-year: 4.942%, up 4.3 basis points.

  • 10-year: 5.138%, up 4.0 basis points.

  • 30-year: 5.471%, up 3.4 basis points.

Last week, the benchmark 10-year yield reached its highest level since March 2002 at 5.365%

.

US homebuilders feel the pressure

The US NAHB housing market index came in at 29, comfortably below the 50 level that separates favorable from unfavorable builder sentiment.

The details showed weakness across all three components:

  • Current sales fell to 33 from 35.

  • Expected sales over the next six months fell to 32 from 37.

  • Prospective buyer traffic fell to 18 from 23.

Builders are working harder to get buyers through the door. Some 43% cut prices in October, the highest share during the 2020–2026 period. The average reduction remained at 6%, while 65% offered sales incentives.

The message? Affordability remains a problem. Builders are cutting prices and offering incentives, but buyer traffic continues to weaken.

Canadian inflation: Energy hotter, core cooler

Canada’s September CPI rose 3.1% year over year versus 3.2% expected and 3.0% previously. Monthly prices increased 0.1%, below the 0.2% estimate.

The headline accelerated, but the underlying details were more encouraging:

  • CPI-median eased to 1.9% from 2.0%.

  • CPI-trim slowed to 1.8% from 1.9%.

  • CPI-common declined to 2.4% from 2.6%.

  • Inflation excluding gasoline slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%.

  • Grocery inflation eased to 1.7% from 2.8%.

Energy remains the problem area, with prices up 19.0% annually and gasoline up 27.8%.

The softer core readings ease pressure on the Bank of Canada to raise rates. USDCAD initially rose from around 1.4075 to 1.4106 after the release. By the European close snapshot, however, it was near 1.4096, still down 0.29% on the day.

Dollar mixed. Gold and oil lower

The dollar was higher against the euro, yen, pound and Swiss franc, but lower against the Canadian, Australian and New Zealand dollars:

  • EURUSD: 1.1204, down 0.31%.

  • USDJPY: 158.51, up 0.33%.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3300, down 0.21%.

  • USDCHF: 0.8268, up 0.35%.

  • USDCAD: 1.4096, down 0.29%.

  • AUDUSD: 0.6975, up 0.45%.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5659, up 0.16%.

In other markets:

  • Crude oil: $98.64, down $0.41 or 0.41%.

  • Gold: $4,140.03, down about $25.10 or 0.60%.

  • Silver: $57.16, up $0.185 or 0.32%.

  • Bitcoin: $81,660, down $342 or 0.42%.

Gold was lower alongside the rise in Treasury yields, while silver managed a modest gain. For European equity buyers, the stronger finish to last week has given way to broad selling to start this one.

item.title: Bank of Canada Q3 business outlook survey -0.33 vs -0.38 prior
item.description:
• BOS indicator -0.33 vs -0.38 in Q2 (revised from -0.39)
  • Future sales balance of opinion +42 vs +15 in Q2
  • 18% of firms report an outright decline in sales over the past 12 months vs 22% in Q2
  • 6% of firms expect a recession in the next year vs 17% in Q2
  • 41% of firms expect inflation above 3% over the next two years vs 44% in Q2
  • Consumers’ 5-year inflation expectations 3.91% vs 3.39% in Q2
  • 53.0% of consumers expect a recession in the next 12 months vs 54.6% in Q2

Roughly three-quarters of the Business Outlook Survey interviews were done before Canada-US trade talks broke down and Ottawa announced new counter-tariffs so this data is already stale. The same goes for the consumer survey, where about three-quarters of responses came in before the August 21 breakdown. I'd argue that the 'breakdown' wasn't that damaging but that's up for debate.

In any case, the snapshot was decent. The jump in the future sales balance to +42 from +15 is a big move, and firms credited an easing of trade tensions and less Middle East risk.

Exporters were leaning on solid US demand and high oil prices. Investment intentions eased only slightly and remain robust. Hiring is the soft spot, with most firms planning to hold headcount flat.

The Bank of Canada addressed the timing problem head-on in a box looking at results collected after the talks collapsed. In the survey view, the new US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs are weighing on outlooks for exports and investment, pushing up costs and prices, and inflation expectations have risen alongside the tariffs and the rebound in energy. The BOC wrote:

Firms surveyed after trade talks broke down reported weaker sentiment and lower expectations for export sales than those surveyed beforehand. These recent results suggest that some of the improvement in firms’ outlooks reported earlier in the third quarter of 2026 has reversed. Nevertheless, sentiment and expectations remain considerably stronger than at the height of trade tensions in 2025, suggesting a moderation rather than a fundamental shift in firms’ outlooks.

Firms’ input and selling price expectations moderated but remain elevated, mostly tied to oil and trade. More worrying for the BoC: companies facing big cost increases plan to keep passing them on, and some see improved demand as the window to claw back margins they gave up earlier. That’s the kind of behaviour that keeps inflation sticky.

Consumer survey 

The real red flag is on the consumer side. Five-year inflation expectations jumped more than half a point to 3.91%, rising to match elevated short-term expectations.

Long-run expectations catching up to short-run ones is exactly the de-anchoring central banks lose sleep over. And again, the BoC says expectations at all horizons moved higher after talks broke down, so the true number is likely worse.

Households reported better financial health thanks to asset gains and a bit more labour market confidence, but spending plans deteriorated from already-weak levels. High prices and uncertainty are the culprits. Interestingly, labour market perceptions improved for workers exposed to US trade but worsened for those in jobs at higher risk of AI task replacement.

Today's CPI data was a good sign for the Bank of Canada but this survey raises some hawkish questions.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin trades in a neutral technical territory as the buyers and sellers continue to resolve their battle
item.description:
Bitcoin made a run higher today, but the buyers have some work to do.

After moving above both its 100- and 200-hour moving averages and reaching $83,075, the price has rotated back between those technical levels. That puts the short-term bias back in neutral territory, with traders waiting for the next shove.

Last week’s rebound stalled below the moving averages

Last week, bitcoin moved higher and found resistance near $84,178. A ceiling was developed at that area, before rotating lower. The decline took the price below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines on the chart below—and into the swing area between $80,106 and $81,183.

Thursday’s low briefly broke below that area, but the sellers could not sustain the momentum. The price snapped back toward the falling moving averages, although it remained below both through the weekend.

The sellers had their shot below support and missed. However, the buyers still needed to get above the moving averages to increase their control.

Today’s break higher loses momentum

That break came today. Bitcoin pushed above:

  • The 100-hour moving average at $81,748.

  • The 200-hour moving average at $82,279.

The move extended to $83,075, with the rebound in stocks potentially helping the risk-on tone. However, the early North American session has seen the price rotate back below the 200-hour moving average and into the gap between the two.

The buyers had their shot above both moving averages, but could not keep the momentum going. Neither side has firm control at the moment.

What would tilt the bias?

On the downside, a break below the 100-hour moving average at $81,748 would tilt the bias back toward the sellers. The next target would be the $80,106–$81,183 swing area. Getting below—and staying below—that area would open the door for further downside momentum.

On the upside, buyers need to reclaim the 200-hour moving average at $82,279 and stay above it. That would put today’s high at $83,075 back in play, followed by last week’s high near $84,178. Above that, the higher swing area between $85,578 and $87,374 becomes the next target.

For now, the immediate battle is between the moving averages. A sustained break outside those levels would give traders a directional bias and a nearby level to define risk.

The broader range going back to mid-September remains in place. Getting out of that range is the bigger challenge. First, traders need to resolve the closer battle.

In the video above, I take a look at the levels that will help define the next move.

item.title: Stock market shows an interesting hidden hint about investor confidence coming into earnings
item.description:
Earnings season heats up: Are investors beginning to reward good results again?

Wall Street's earnings season began cautiously, with investors punishing disappointments more severely than they rewarded positive surprises. But fresh trading activity on October 19 suggests that sentiment may be stabilizing. With Netflix, Tesla and Meta preparing to report, the next question is whether investors are becoming more willing to reward strong corporate results, or whether this improvement is only temporary.

Early earnings reactions were more negative than positive

The third-quarter earnings reporting season, taking place during the fourth quarter of 2026, began with some uncomfortable signals for stock market bulls.

An investingLive review of earnings reactions from October 13-16 identified several signs of a selective and defensive market:

  • Three of the four trading sessions produced negative capitalization-weighted earnings reactions, meaning larger companies had a greater influence on the results.

  • Downside moves exceeding options-implied expectations outnumbered upside surprises by 11 to 6.

  • Investors were not consistently rewarding corporate earnings announcements, even as individual companies continued reporting solid business performance.

These observations matter because good earnings are not necessarily enough to make a stock rise.

A company may report higher revenue, stronger profits and encouraging business developments, yet still see its shares decline.

Why?

Because stock prices reflect expectations about the future, not just the financial results being announced today. If investors were already expecting an exceptional quarter, a merely good quarter may disappoint.

The opposite can also happen. A company with relatively modest results may see its shares rally if investors feared something much worse.

October 19: The first encouraging signs?

The latest October 19 intraday earnings reactions offer a somewhat more constructive picture.

Among six companies with usable earnings reactions in the supplied investingLive analysis:

  • Four stocks advanced, while two declined.

  • Positive breadth reached 66.7%, meaning two-thirds of the companies gained.

  • The capitalization-weighted reaction was approximately +1.20%.

  • None of the five companies with comparable options-implied expected moves had exceeded its estimated range at the observation time.

This is an improvement worth watching, but not yet a decisive turnaround.

The most interesting distinction is that stocks were rising without necessarily producing unusually large upside surprises.

An options-implied move is an estimate of how far a stock might move around an event, inferred from options prices. When a stock moves beyond that range, the reaction may indicate that investors are repricing the company more dramatically than the options market had anticipated.

October 19's early data shows more stocks participating on the upside, but not yet evidence of exceptional positive repricing.

That difference matters.

It could be the beginning of stabilization. Alternatively, it could simply represent a relatively favorable collection of companies reporting on one particular day.

The October 19 observations are intraday snapshots, not final closing returns. The sample is also small and has not established a confirmed change in the broader earnings environment.

Cleveland-Cliffs and Fifth Third offer encouraging examples

Two companies illustrate how different types of corporate results can attract buyers.

Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF): A stronger outlook captures attention

The steel producer's shares were up approximately 7.84% in the supplied October 19 intraday snapshot.

Cleveland-Cliffs reported a substantial improvement in third-quarter profitability and presented a more optimistic earnings outlook. That combination gives investors something beyond the reported quarter to assess: whether the company's future profitability may improve more than previously expected.

The relevant question now is whether buyers maintain their enthusiasm beyond the immediate reaction.

A strong first-day gain is encouraging, but holding that gain over subsequent sessions would provide stronger evidence of sustained investor interest.

Fifth Third Bancorp (FITB): Banking resilience gets a measured response

Fifth Third gained approximately 1.42% in the supplied snapshot.

The regional banking group reported resilient credit performance, sequential growth in net interest income and progress integrating Comerica.

Its more measured share-price reaction illustrates another aspect of this earnings season: investors may be receptive to improving fundamentals without necessarily bidding shares sharply higher.

Elsewhere, the picture remains mixed. Recent rolling weekly performance has been comparatively strong for Ericsson, while Charles Schwab, Interactive Brokers and Prologis have experienced further weakness.

Those weekly returns are not isolated earnings reactions, but they reinforce the importance of evaluating individual companies rather than assuming that the entire market is moving together.

Netflix earnings on October 20: A test of expectations

Netflix (NFLX) reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, October 20.

Investors will be examining whether the streaming company can sustain growth while defending profitability and maintaining engagement in an increasingly competitive entertainment market.

The important questions include:

Engagement and revenue: Is Netflix generating sufficient revenue growth from its audience, advertising business and programming investments?

Profitability: Can the company maintain attractive margins while competing for viewers and spending on content?

Guidance: Does management's outlook support the growth expectations already embedded in the share price?

Even a headline earnings beat may not be enough if management's forward outlook disappoints.

For existing shareholders, the result may help assess whether the longer-term investment thesis remains intact. For traders, the initial share-price reaction and its ability to hold could be just as informative as the reported numbers themselves.

Tesla and Meta on October 21: Two different tests of investor confidence

Wednesday brings two major earnings announcements, each carrying broader market implications.

Tesla (TSLA): How much future growth is already priced in?

Tesla investors face several important questions, including automotive profitability, demand, energy storage growth and investment in future technologies.

The company's October 2 delivery report showed more than 486,000 vehicles delivered during the third quarter. However, vehicle deliveries alone do not establish profitability.

Investors will want to understand how sales volumes translate into margins, cash flow and management's outlook.

A strong reaction could indicate that investors are willing to look beyond near-term spending pressures. A disappointing reaction could suggest that the market is becoming less patient with ambitious future-growth expectations.

Meta Platforms (META): Is AI spending delivering sufficient returns?

Meta presents a different challenge.

Its advertising business provides an established source of profitability, while investment in artificial intelligence and supporting infrastructure creates additional spending demands.

The central question is whether advertising growth and business efficiency are sufficient to justify the scale of investment.

Positive operating results accompanied by higher spending projections could produce a complicated market response.

Strong profitability, credible guidance and evidence that investment is creating value would provide a more constructive combination.

Because these businesses influence major stock indices, their earnings reactions could also affect sentiment beyond their own shareholders.

What could confirm an improving earnings environment?

Rather than declaring earnings season bullish or bearish based on one favorable session, traders and investors can watch for three developments.

1. More stocks rising after earnings

If positive breadth persists across a larger and more diverse group of reporting companies, it would strengthen the case that investor sentiment is improving.

2. More meaningful upside reactions

Positive share-price moves are encouraging. But repeated moves exceeding options-implied expectations would suggest investors are becoming more willing to revalue companies upward.

3. Stocks holding their gains

One of the most useful tests comes after the initial excitement.

If a stock rallies following earnings and retains much of that advance over the following sessions, it suggests that buyers are continuing to support the new valuation.

Conversely, repeated reversals of initial rallies would indicate that enthusiasm remains fragile.

The same principle applies to negative reactions. A stock that initially falls but subsequently recovers can provide evidence that sellers are losing influence, although one recovery alone does not prove a durable bottom.

What if the improvement fails?

There is an important alternative scenario.

October 19's stronger reactions could prove temporary, especially if upcoming large-company reports disappoint investors.

Warning signs would include a renewed deterioration in earnings-reaction breadth, more stocks falling beyond their expected trading ranges, and strong companies struggling to hold gains after reporting.

The next wave of technology earnings will provide important evidence.

Microsoft and Alphabet are scheduled to report on October 28, followed by Amazon on October 29. Their cloud operations, AI-related investment and profitability outlooks will offer additional insight into how investors are assessing some of the market's most influential businesses.

The key takeaway for traders and investors

The most useful question this earnings season may not be simply, "Did the company beat expectations?"

It may be:

"Did investors reward the results, and did they continue to reward them after the initial reaction?"

For existing shareholders, earnings provide an opportunity to reassess business fundamentals, valuation and the longer-term investment case. A short-term price decline does not automatically invalidate an otherwise sound business thesis.

For traders and investors considering new positions, it can be useful to distinguish the immediate reaction from subsequent price behavior. A sharp move can create an opportunity, but it can also introduce significant risk when volatility and uncertainty are elevated.

As of October 19, the earnings environment remains selective, with tentative signs of stabilization rather than a confirmed bullish shift.

Netflix, Tesla and Meta may provide some of the clearest evidence yet of whether investors are becoming more willing to reward good corporate performance.

And for the broader stock market, that distinction could matter more than the number of companies that beat analysts' estimates.

item.title: US NAHB housing market index 29 vs 31 prior
item.description:
• Priorw as 32
  • Current sales 33 vs 35 prior
  • Sales over the next six months 32 vs 37 prior
  • Prospective buyers 18 vs 23 prior

The latest survey found that 43% of builders cut prices in October, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period. The average price cut remained at 6% for the seventh consecutive month. Meanwhile, 65% of builders reported using sales incentives in October, the 19th straight month at least 60% of builders have done so.

This is a response to yet-another rise in borrowing costs, with US mortages nearing 7.5% on a 30-year fixed in the period.

For background, The NAHB Housing Market Index is a monthly survey of homebuilder sentiment published by the National Association of Home Builders. It’s released around mid-month at 10 am ET, usually the day before the government’s housing starts report, which makes it the earliest read on the US housing market each month.

The index is built from a survey of NAHB members, focused on builders of single-family homes. They rate three conditions: current sales of new homes, expected sales over the next six months and traffic of prospective buyers. The responses are combined into a headline index running from 0 to 100. A reading of 50 is the dividing line, with anything above it meaning more builders view conditions as good than poor. The traffic component historically runs well below the other two and rarely tops 50 even in strong markets. NAHB also publishes regional readings for the Northeast, Midwest, South and West as three-month moving averages.

In recent years the survey’s added questions on price cuts and sales incentives have become some of its most useful details. They show how much builders are discounting or buying down mortgage rates to keep homes moving, information the headline doesn’t capture.

The index is highly sensitive to mortgage rates and affordability, and it tends to lead housing starts and building permits. It rarely moves broader markets on its own, but it’s watched closely by homebuilder stocks and as an early signal for residential investment, a key swing factor in GDP. Builders’ commentary on construction costs, including lumber, materials and tariffs, also feeds into the inflation picture.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

The broader market helps define the roadmap

Individual stocks have their own stories. Earnings, company news and sector developments can all drive price action. However, the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 give traders a broader view of market sentiment.

That perspective matters. Is your stock moving higher with support from the broader market? Or is it trying to rally while the major indices remain under pressure?

The same technical tools apply to both: moving averages, swing areas and retracement levels help define the bias, the risk and the next targets. Looking at the broader indices alongside an individual stock can make the trading roadmap clearer.

What has today’s rebound changed?

A higher price is a start, but where the price trades relative to key technical levels tells us more. Have the buyers taken back control? Are they testing resistance? Or do the sellers still have the stronger hand despite today’s gains?

The buyers are making a push. The technical levels will help tell us how much progress they are making, but understand there is work to do to erase some of the sharp declines seen last week. Watch and learn.

item.title: USDCAD bounces after softer CPI data but they have work to do.
item.description:
Canada’s September CPI report gave traders a little something on both sides of the inflation debate.

Headline inflation rose to 3.1% year over year from 3.0% in August, but came in below expectations of 3.2%. Meanwhile, inflation excluding gasoline slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%.

Energy remains the problem area. Gasoline prices increased 27.8% from a year earlier, while fuel oil and other fuels surged 57.8%, with a greater impact on households in Atlantic Canada. Shelter inflation also accelerated, although rent growth held steady and mortgage interest costs continued to decline.

The better news came from groceries. Annual inflation slowed to 1.7%, the lowest since May 2024, with fresh vegetables and sugar and confectionery prices declining from a year earlier. That is welcome relief, but slower inflation does not undo the earlier increases. Grocery prices remain 33.0% above September 2020 levels.

What does it mean for the Bank of Canada?

The headline moved higher, but energy drove the acceleration. The question for the Bank of Canada is whether those higher costs spread into other prices.

Slower inflation excluding gasoline offers some reassurance. However, the 0.4% seasonally adjusted monthly increase warrants attention.

For currency traders, higher inflation would normally support Canadian yields and the Canadian dollar, putting downward pressure on USDCAD. The softer-than-expected headline and slower non-gasoline inflation temper that argument.

So, what are the technicals telling traders?

Sellers have control. Can buyers defend 1.4082?

USDCAD moved lower ahead of the report, reaching a session low of 1.4071. That took the price below the 38.2% retracement at 1.40818 of the rally from the August 21 low to the October highs near 1.42984.

Following the report, the price recovered to 1.41119, but that bounce faded. The pair is back below 1.4100, trading near 1.4095.

For buyers, holding above 1.40818 is the first requirement. It gives them a level to lean against and define risk. It does not, by itself, put them in control.

A move back below that level—and staying below—would keep the sellers firmly in charge. The session low at 1.4071 would come back into focus, followed by the 100-day moving average at 1.40377. The price has not traded below that moving average since September 16.

Broken support becomes resistance

On the topside, buyers first need to get above the post-report corrective high near 1.4112.

Above that sits a more important swing area between 1.41297 and 1.41532. That zone has defined turning points going back to November 2025 and again between June 19 and July 14 this year.

The price broke above it on September 28. Now that USDCAD is back below, what was support becomes resistance.

Getting above that area—and staying above—would give buyers a stronger say in the direction.

Right now, however, they have work to do. Sellers remain in control, and 1.4082 is the short-term barometer. Stay above, and buyers can try to build a recovery. Move below, and the door opens for another shove lower.

In the video, I walk through the levels that define the risk, the bias, and the next targets for USDCAD.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada September CPI 3.1% y/y vs 3.2% expected
item.description:
• Prior was 3.0%
  • CPI +0.1% m/m vs +0.2% expected
  • BOC core 2.2% y/y vs 2.4% prior
  • BOC core 0.0% m/m vs +0.1% prior
  • CPI median 1.9% vs 1.9% expected (prior was 2.0%)
  • CPI trim 1.8% vs 1.9% expected (prior was 1.9%)
  • CPI common 2.4% vs 2.6% prior

This is a good report from the Bank of Canada and should ease pressure on them to hike rates. At the same time, that's a negative for the Canadian dollar and we quickly saw USD/CAD rose to 1.4106 from 1.4075.

USDCAD 10 mins:

Details:

  • Energy: +19.0% y/y vs +15.4% prior
  • Gasoline: +27.8% y/y vs +22.8% prior
  • Selter 1.8% y/y
  • Services 2.6% y/y
  • Food from stores: +1.7% y/y vs +2.8% prior -- lowest since May 2024
  • Ex gasoline 2.2% vs 2.4% prior
  • On a monthly basis, both trim and median rose about 0.18%, which annualizes to roughly 2.2%

For background, Statistics Canada publishes the Consumer Price Index monthly, usually in the third week of the following month at 8:30 am ET. It measures price changes for a fixed basket of goods and services bought by Canadian households, covering shelter, food, transportation, household operations, clothing, health, recreation and alcohol and tobacco.

Unlike in the US, the market’s focus is the year-over-year change in the unadjusted index rather than the seasonally adjusted monthly change, though both are published. The Bank of Canada targets 2% total CPI inflation, the midpoint of a 1% to 3% control range, and its mandate is framed around that headline measure.

Because headline inflation can be distorted by volatile items like gasoline and food, the Bank also watches its preferred core measures, CPI-trim and CPI-median. CPI-trim excludes the components with the most extreme price moves each month. CPI-median takes the price change at the 50th percentile of the basket. Markets often look at the average of the two. Other core gauges include CPIX and CPI excluding food and energy.

Shelter is the largest component and a frequent source of noise. It includes mortgage interest cost, which creates a quirk in the data: when the Bank raises interest rates, mortgage costs rise and push measured inflation higher, at least temporarily. Rent and homeowners’ replacement cost are also closely watched.

Canadian CPI is one of the most market-moving domestic releases, with surprises in the core measures in particular able to shift Bank of Canada rate pricing and move the Canadian dollar. With the US the dominant trading partner, tariffs and exchange-rate swings have become an important channel for imported inflation

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar mixed as US–Iran hopes weigh on oil; Nasdaq futures rise
item.description:

item.title: Why do central banks target 2% inflation instead of 0%?
item.description:
Most major central banks have a clearly defined inflation target around 2% per year over the medium term. But why they don't aim for 0%, so that prices remain unchanged over time?  The answer lies in how inflation expectations influence economic decisions, the risks associated with deflation and the limitations of monetary policy.

An inflation target provides a clear reference point for households, businesses and financial markets. This matters because expectations influence behaviour. Businesses consider expected inflation when setting prices and negotiating wages. Workers take expected changes in the cost of living into account when negotiating salaries. Households factor expected inflation into decisions about consumption, saving and borrowing, while investors incorporate it into bond yields and other asset prices.

When the public trusts that a central bank will keep inflation close to its target, expectations are more likely to remain anchored around that level. This helps prevent temporary price shocks from turning into persistent inflation.

Take the increase in oil prices as an example. Higher energy costs can push headline inflation up temporarily. If households and businesses believe the central bank will bring inflation back towards 2%, they may be less inclined to demand permanently higher wages or raise prices aggressively in anticipation of further inflation. This makes the initial shock less likely to spread throughout the economy.

The opposite can happen when confidence in the inflation target deteriorates. If workers expect prices to keep rising, they may demand larger wage increases. Businesses facing higher labour costs may then raise their prices, reinforcing inflationary pressures. Central banks may have to raise interest rates more aggressively to break this cycle.

An inflation target acts as an anchor for expectations. It does not eliminate economic shocks, but it can help prevent those shocks from becoming self-reinforcing.

Why target 2% instead of 0%?

There are several reasons why a modestly positive inflation rate is preferable. The first is to create a buffer against deflation. Deflation occurs when the general price level falls persistently. Although falling prices might initially seem beneficial to consumers, widespread and sustained deflation can create serious economic problems.

When people expect prices to fall further, they may postpone purchases. Businesses can respond to weaker demand by reducing investment, cutting production and laying off workers. Lower incomes can then weaken demand further, putting additional downward pressure on prices and the economy.

Deflation also increases the real burden of debt. A household or business that borrowed money must still repay the same nominal amount, even if the prices of the goods and services it sells are falling. Revenues and wages may decline while debt repayments remain unchanged, making existing loans more difficult to service.

This can create a damaging feedback loop between falling prices, weaker demand, declining incomes and financial stress. A 2% inflation target provides a margin of safety. Inflation fluctuates around its target as the economy experiences changes in demand, supply disruptions and other shocks. If the target were 0%, a relatively small negative shock could push the economy into deflation immediately. With a positive target, central banks have more room to absorb these fluctuations without falling into deflation.

Inflation and real interest rates

Another reason central banks target positive inflation is that it helps preserve room to stimulate the economy by lowering real interest rates. What matters for economic activity is not just the nominal interest rate set by a central bank, but also how that rate compares with inflation. Real interest rates measure the cost of borrowing after accounting for the erosion of purchasing power caused by inflation. The real interest rate is approximately the nominal interest rate minus expected inflation.

When inflation exceeds the nominal interest rate, real interest rates are negative. This makes borrowing relatively cheap in real terms and reduces the real burden of existing nominal debt, supporting consumption, investment and credit growth. Conversely, when nominal interest rates exceed inflation, real rates are positive, making borrowing more expensive in real terms and encouraging saving over spending. This tends to restrain demand and slow economic activity.

Central banks therefore influence the economy partly by adjusting nominal rates relative to inflation expectations. When growth weakens, they can cut nominal rates to reduce real borrowing costs and provide stimulus. However, their ability to do so becomes more constrained when nominal rates are already close to zero.

This is where a positive inflation target becomes important. If inflation expectations are anchored around 2%, nominal interest rates can generally settle at a higher level over time than they would in an economy with a 0% inflation target, all else being equal. This gives central banks more room to cut nominal rates during a downturn, lowering real rates and making monetary conditions more accommodative.

A zero inflation target would leave less of a buffer against deflation. If inflation expectations fell below zero while nominal rates were already near zero, real interest rates could rise even without any increase in nominal rates. Monetary conditions would become more restrictive precisely when the economy might need additional support. This is what happened during the Great Depression as deflation drove real interest rates higher and made the economic downturn much worse.

A positive inflation target helps reduce this risk. It does not guarantee that real rates will always be low enough to stimulate growth, but it provides a buffer against deflation and gives central banks more flexibility to lower real borrowing costs when economic conditions deteriorate.

item.title: Connecting the dots: What falling luxury sales could be telling us about the US economy
item.description:
When most people look at designer bags, what do you think is the first thought that comes to mind? I'd wager it would be along the lines of "nice, but absolutely not at that price". And that very moment of hesitation could actually tell us more about the economy than you might think.

Now, a luxury bag isn't like groceries or petrol. It is a want, not a need. But when people start thinking twice about those purchases, it is worth thinking about the bigger picture and whether consumer confidence is taking a hit.

According to Citi's credit card data released earlier this month, luxury spending fell 6% year-on-year in September. And that follows from the declines of 4% in both July and August before that. The data shows three consecutive months of weakness. So, that is not exactly encouraging especially when wealthy US consumers have been one of the more resilient groups in this economy.

Having said that, let's take a look at this. US retail sales actually rose by 0.8% in September, albeit largely bolstered by higher gasoline prices. But in excluding gasoline stations, retail sales still grew by 0.2%.

It's not extravagant but it still suggests that US consumers are still spending. However, that doesn't necessarily mean they are buying more stuff. It just means that their spending habits have perhaps changed.

So, how does this tie back to Wall Street?

Just imagine that you are running a luxury retailer. You've got expensive stores, employees and marketing bills to pay. And those costs don't disappear just because fewer customers are buying handbags. As such, slower sales mean less revenue to cover those expenses. And if you turn to promotions to attract customers, then your profit margins could get squeezed further.

Now, I'm not suggesting fewer handbag purchases mean a recession is coming. Luxury spending is only one piece of the consumer puzzle, and the wealthiest shoppers tend to behave differently from everyone else.

But if that hesitation starts spreading to the likes of clothing, electronics, travel and other discretionary purchases, then corporate earnings forecasts could be next in line for a reality check. And when investors start questioning how much consumers are really willing to spend, stock valuations can suddenly look rather expensive.

With that in mind, it's worth noting that sometimes the first economic warning can simply just be what is sitting unsold on a store shelf. And it could very well be the designer bag that the crowd chooses to pass on.

item.title: Economic data spotlight: UK inflation set to climb as BOE rate hike and autumn budget collide
item.description:
There's going to be plenty of watchful eyes on the UK CPI report this Wednesday, not least with the autumn budget just around the corner. Another hot set of inflation numbers could very well make life rather uncomfortable for both the government and the BOE.

The headline annual inflation estimate is expected to rise to 3.4% in September, up from 3.1% in August. Meanwhile, core annual inflation is expected to also climb to 2.8% in September - up from 2.6% in the month before.

All in all, that would take inflation further away from the BOE's 2% target, with higher energy costs continuing to put pressure on household budgets. At the same time, services inflation continues to be sticky and remains a problem for policymakers in trying to bring down broader price pressures in the UK economy.

And while the UK economy isn't exactly falling apart, consumer demand remains fragile and the labour market has been showing signs of strain.

The August GDP estimate may have surprised with 0.1% growth, but that was largely driven by the production side as services output was flat on the month. Meanwhile, the latest labour market snapshot showed that payrolls continued to fall in August - marking a 0.5% drop in the past year alone. The unemployment rate for July was seen at 4.9%, also up by 0.2% from the past year.

So, that's making for a bit of an awkward combination for the BOE. It isn't all too worrying now but it could grow to be even more so if the diverging trends keep up.

For now, traders are already pricing in roughly 95% odds of a 25 bps rate hike for 5 November with another 25 bps increase priced by February next year. From that, the immediate move looks almost settled. The major worry right now I would say is whether the inflation trend will strengthen the case for further tightening.

But before we get to the BOE, there's the 28 October budget to deal with first right after the inflation data this week.

UK chancellor Healey is vowing to provide relief to struggling households while keeping borrowing and gilt yields under control. So, higher inflation will just make that balancing act much harder. Additional fiscal support might cushion the energy shock, but an expensive package that unsettles bond investors could push borrowing costs higher anyway.

That is quite a lot of things all taking place in the span of the next two weeks.

A hotter-than-expected UK CPI report could reinforce expectations for further BOE tightening, even as higher interest rates squeeze households and businesses. On the flip side, a softer reading might offer some relief but it likely won't be enough to make UK's fiscal problems disappear.

Markets may be bracing themselves already for a November rate hike, but the real question that traders need to be concerned about is how much more tightening the UK economy can afford.

item.title: Chart of the day: France's bond market is flashing another warning for EUR/USD
item.description:
It's a brand new week, but same old problem for the euro. Once again, it is France that is giving the single currency yet another headache.

The weekend riots across the country have piled more pressure on Macron's government, just as investors are already questioning whether France can get its fiscal house in order. And the bond market is signaling that there isn't much assurance of that, as the yield spread between French and German 10-year bonds has widened back towards 145 bps. That now draws the 150 bps mark back in the picture.

This once again continues to reaffirm where the pressure point is for the European bond market, with the spread having just hovered around 85 bps at the beginning of September.

France is already struggling with a ballooning fiscal deficit, political fragmentation, and a very difficult path towards budget consolidation. As such, the latest unrest only makes it harder for the government to push through unpopular spending cuts.

So, where does that leave the euro?

Well, EUR/USD is slipping back towards the 1.1200 level with sellers still firmly in control as price action continues to rest well below the 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages.

A firm break below 1.1200 would expose the October low around 1.1113 next, while any meaningful recovery needs to first get back above 1.1250 with the 23.6 Fib retracement level at around 1.1254 reinforcing the first resistance layer for the pair. After which, the 38.2 Fib retracement level closer to 1.1341 may come into play.

For now, the bigger risk here is that France's troubles may be starting to spill over into broader euro area bond markets. If so, that could turn what is currently a French political problem into something much more uncomfortable for the euro.

If the French-German yield spread at 150 bps gives way, I reckon the euro will be in for a very rough ride as get into the latter stages of October trading. As an aside, just be wary that Moody's is set to review France's credit rating on 23 October. So, that's another potential catalyst looming for euro traders.

item.title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Meta faces a $145 billion question after the tech rout
item.description:
The tech rout last week has certainly come at a rather interesting time for markets. While it was on the back of hotter-than-expected inflation data, the reaction was one that ran against the bond market as Treasury yields fell sharply last week. As such, it definitely begs the question as to whether there is some other underlying factor driving the retreat in tech stocks in particular.

Is it a case that investors are waking up to the struggles in the market breadth and momentum? Or is it investors simply asking the question of whether all the AI spending is actually going to pay off?

With that in mind, there's certainly a lot on the line as we look to the earnings calendar this week. And among the big tech names, Meta is arguably my pick on what will really stand out against the above backdrop.

The Nasdaq already slumped by over 4% last week and despite futures posting a modest bounce to start the new week, the underlying sentiment remains shaky. So, another strong earnings report might not necessarily be enough to win investors over this time.

Analysts are expecting revenue of around $63.3 billion, up 24% from a year ago, alongside earnings of $5.60 per share. The latter would be a massive jump from the $1.05 reported last year, although that comparison is distorted by a $15.9 billion one-off tax charge in the previous period.

However, I would argue that the bigger story isn't really about whether Meta beats those estimates. As we have seen with many of these big tech earnings releases, it's all about how much money these companies are spending to keep their AI ambitions alive. And it will be the same story for Meta this week as well.

The firm had previously said that they are planning to spend between $130 billion and $145 billion on capital expenditures this year. Now, that is a rather staggering amount and we're also seeing that show up in terms of financial impact.

In the second quarter, revenue grew 28% but operating expenses jumped 55%, partly due to legal and restructuring charges. Meanwhile, operating margins fell to 31% from 43% a year earlier, with free cash flow dwindling to just $784 million from $8.55 billion.

Don't get me wrong. Meta's advertising business is still performing strongly. However, there's a difference between having a profitable business to fund AI investments and proving that those investments are actually worth the money.

As such, that is where the outlook for 2027 will be a key focus to watch. Some Wall Street estimates are already suggesting that capital spending could climb towards $190 billion to $225 billion next year. But really, how much longer can that spending keep growing before investors demand clearer returns?

It's an argument that we have all been harping on since the start of this year already and with every quarter that goes by, we are surely getting closer and closer to knocking down that door.

And with Treasury yields still elevated, investors may have lesser and lesser room to be less forgiving of expensive AI promises. With that in mind, I reckon Meta will need to offer more than another upbeat outlook to really keep investors assured.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Brokers must look beyond the crypto hype to where trading demand lies, says IC
item.description:
The growing attention surrounding cryptocurrencies should not distract brokers from the markets their clients continue to trade, according to Jason Hughes, General Manager at IC.

Speaking at iFX EXPO Asia 2026 in Hong Kong, Hughes joined industry executives to debate whether digital assets are delivering on their commercial promise, or whether established markets such as gold, precious metals and major FX pairs remain the backbone of the brokerage business.

The discussion, “From Bitcoin to Bullion: Where Is the Real Revenue?”, examined a question facing brokers across Asia and beyond: where should firms direct their next round of investment as client demand, trading technology and market conditions change?

“For brokers, the priority is not choosing between traditional and digital assets. It is ensuring clients can access the markets they want to trade, supported by reliable infrastructure and consistent execution standards,” Hughes said.

While digital assets have opened new opportunities for brokers, the discussion also raised questions about the commercial case for investing in new products and technologies, particularly when established instruments continue to attract trading activity.

The panel examined the challenges of 24/7 trading, from liquidity provision to execution quality, and the implications for brokers expanding their product offerings.

For Hughes, the wider issue is how firms balance innovation with the fundamentals of their business. New products may attract attention, but their long-term value depends on client demand and the infrastructure needed to support trading activity.

Hughes also took part in “Inside the Deal: The Future of Financial Brands in Sport”, a separate discussion on the commercial value of sports partnerships.

Drawing on IC's involvement in motorsport and esports, he discussed why financial brands need to look beyond sponsorship exposure and consider how partnerships support their broader business objectives.

“The value of a sports partnership goes beyond visibility. It comes from the relationships you build, the audiences you reach and the trust you develop over time,” Hughes said.

He noted that while brand awareness remains important, its direct commercial impact can be difficult to isolate. For IC, engagement with business partners and the opportunity to build relationships are also important measures of value.

item.title: Gold eyes another run at $4,200 but the bond market still holds the key
item.description:
Gold looks poised to make another run at the $4,200 mark to start the new week, with buyers finding some encouragement from falling Treasury yields and softer oil prices. While the bounce since the second half of last week looks encouraging, I would argue that the bond market will still have the final say on whether this recovery has more room to run.

Looking at the daily chart, we can see that gold has been trying to establish a base around $4,100 after the sharp retreat in late September. The drop is also somewhat defended by technical support from the 78.6 Fib retracement level around $4,117. And while buyers have managed to keep price action supported above that level, they haven't quite found enough conviction to firmly push back above $4,200.

As such, that is making for a rather cagey technical setup at the moment.

A firm break above $4,200 would be a welcome first step for buyers, but there is the 100-day moving average (red line) to get through next around $4,239. But if that clears, buyers can at least start to take a look at a run towards the swing region around $4,300-20 next.

So, what's stopping gold buyers from building further momentum at this stage?

Well, the recent retreat in Treasury yields has definitely afforded the non-yielding precious metal a bit of a breather. 10-year yields have slipped back towards 5.06% today but the prospect of higher inflation pressures hasn't exactly gone away. The hotter-than-expected US inflation readings last week continue to keep the pressure on the Fed outlook with traders still widely anticipating another rate hike by year-end. While October might be off the table, Fed funds futures show that traders are pricing in roughly 90% odds of another rate hike in December.

And despite 10-year Treasury yields easing back, they are still at an elevated level considering that they are holding above 5%. As such, that does present stiff competition for an asset like gold - that offers no yield of its own.

For now, the $4,100 level remains the key downside support to watch. A break below that has the potential to expose gold towards a run at the psychological $4,000 mark again. But seeing as how the precious metal is sticking with the bounce from the end of last week, buyers may well get another opportunity to challenge $4,200 first this week. But unless Treasury yields can sustain their latest retreat, it would be tough to bet on any lasting technical breakout for gold just yet.
